lesson.title: Where the Slope's Standard Error Actually Comes From
lesson.summary: The standard error of the slope measures how much a sample slope would vary across repeated samples, built from the leftover scatter in the residuals and the spread of the x-values.
lesson.body:
The last chapter used SE(b1) ≈ 0.1069 without explaining where it came from. Time to open that box. A standard error, in general, measures how much a statistic would bounce around from one random sample to the next. For the slope specifically, two separate things control how much bounce there is: how much scatter is left over after the line is fit (the residuals), and how spread out the x-values are. Tight, consistent points close to the line produce a slope you can pin down precisely; x-values that are all bunched close together make the line's tilt hard to estimate confidently, even if the points sit right on it.

The formula packages both of those ideas: SE(b1) = s / sqrt(SSxx). Here s is the residual standard deviation, s = sqrt(SSE / (n − 2)), where SSE is the sum of squared residuals, the typical size of a leftover vertical miss between a data point and the line. SSxx is the sum of squared deviations of x from its mean, sum of (xi − mean of x)^2, a measure of how spread out the x-values are.

Back to the six students. The residuals (actual score minus predicted score) are: 0 at x = 1, 0.2 at x = 2, −0.6 at x = 3, 0.6 at x = 4, −0.2 at x = 5, and 0 at x = 6. Squaring and adding: 0² + 0.2² + (−0.6)² + 0.6² + (−0.2)² + 0² = 0 + 0.04 + 0.36 + 0.36 + 0.04 + 0 = 0.8. That's SSE. With df = 4, s = sqrt(0.8 / 4) = sqrt(0.2) ≈ 0.4472.

For SSxx, the deviations of x = 1 through 6 from the mean 3.5 are −2.5, −1.5, −0.5, 0.5, 1.5, 2.5. Squaring and adding gives 6.25 + 2.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 2.25 + 6.25 = 17.5, so sqrt(SSxx) = sqrt(17.5) ≈ 4.1833. Putting it together: SE(b1) = 0.4472 / 4.1833 ≈ 0.1069, exactly the value used to build last chapter's t-statistic of 16.84.

The interpretation: if this study were repeated over and over with fresh samples of six students, drawn from the same population and following the same true relationship, the sample slope would typically differ from one repetition to the next by around 0.107 points-per-hour, purely from the luck of who got sampled. Notice what would make that number bigger: messier data (larger residuals, bigger s) or x-values crammed into a narrower range (smaller SSxx). Either change would inflate SE(b1) and shrink the resulting t-statistic, even with the exact same slope of 1.8, which is exactly why a small SE(b1) here is what let last chapter's t-statistic come out so large.
